column3: White oak clear wood, green-to-ovendry dimensional change
column4: FPL-GTR-282 Chapter 4, Table 4-3, Oak, white/White, p. 4-8; https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/62243.pdf
column5: Radial, tangential and volumetric shrinkage are separate tabulated species averages, expressed as percentages of the green dimension or volume. They are total green-to-ovendry parameters, not measured shrinkage at every moisture content. The 0-30 percent moisture applicability permits their use in the approximate Equation (4-9) model with the separately declared 30 percent fiber-saturation approximation. The source reports about 15 percent coefficient of variation for shrinkage generally, not per-value uncertainty; uncertainty remains Unstated. No longitudinal shrinkage, same-specimen covariance, graded-lumber qualification or temperature dependence is supplied.

column3: White oak clear wood with prescribed uniform dry-basis moisture content
column4: FPL-GTR-282 Chapter 4, Equation (4-9) and accompanying text, p. 4-10; https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/62243.pdf
column5: The source permits 30 percent moisture as an approximation when the fiber saturation point is unknown; this value is an explicit engineering assumption, not a measured species-specific fiber saturation point. Below fiber saturation, S(M)=S0*(1-M/0.30), with moisture and shrinkage as fractions. The linear approximation assumes a sufficiently small piece without significant moisture gradients. The existing density at 12 percent remains its independent reference observation; prescribed-moisture density must account separately for water mass and the independently tabulated volumetric shrinkage. No moisture transport, drying rate or coupled thermal-density law is supplied.

column3: White oak, the White species row within the white-oak group; clear straight-grained small specimens at 12 percent moisture content
column4: FPL-GTR-282 Table 5-3a, Oak/white/White, 12% row; definitions in chapter 5 and table footnotes
column5: Species averages, not pooled white-oak-group values, graded lumber or structural design allowables. Specific gravity uses ovendry mass divided by volume at 12% moisture; density = 1000 * 0.68 * 1.12 = 761.6 kg/m3. Bending MOE includes shear deflection at span/depth 14; longitudinal modulus is the source's approximate 10% correction, 1.1 * 12300 = 13530 MPa. MOR is a bending failure index, not uniaxial tensile strength. Compression perpendicular is stress at proportional limit, not ultimate strength; shear and perpendicular tension average radial and tangential tests. Side hardness is modified-Janka force for half-diameter penetration of an 11.28 mm ball, not pressure. The separately tabulated white-oak elastic ratios are not joined because their group/species population is not identified. Temperature and uncertainty are unspecified. No full stiffness tensor, moisture/temperature extrapolation, heat capacity, conductivity, loss or fracture law is supplied.

column3: White oak clear wood at fixed 12 percent dry-basis moisture content
column5: Engineering correlations, not additional species measurements or graded-lumber data. Cp in J/(kg K) is 1000*((0.1031+0.003867*T+4.18*0.12)/1.12+12*(-0.06191+0.000236*T-0.000133*12)); its fixed-moisture dependence is affine in absolute T over 280-420 K, so linear interpolation reproduces this model. Transverse conductivity at 297.15 K is G12*(0.1941+0.004064*12)+0.01864 using this bundle's ovendry-mass/volume-at-12-percent G12=0.68. The conductivity correlation requires G12>0.3 and MC<25 percent; the source reports actual conductivity may differ by 20 percent, which is not a statistical confidence interval. No longitudinal conductivity, moisture evolution, drying, phase change, pressure dependence, thermal-density law or temperature extension of the mechanical measurements is supplied.
